title: Kosher Kilimanjaro: Full Guide
excerpt: You can climb Kilimanjaro without breaking Shabbat or kashrut. The guide: a schedule around two Shabbatot, food on the mountain, prayer at altitude.
seoTitle: Kosher Kilimanjaro: Climbing with Shabbat and Kashrut

content.value: On Friday at midday, at Mweka Gate, 1,640 m above sea level, our Shabbat-observant group finishes its climb. A few hours later the Shabbat candles are already lit in Arusha. Yes, you can climb to the summit of Kilimanjaro, 5,895 m, without walking a single step on Shabbat and without eating a single dish that is not kosher. The condition is planning: a route that fits exactly between two Shabbatot, a kosher kitchen that goes up the mountain with the group, and prayer that fits the rhythm of the trekking days.

Most guides to Kilimanjaro do not mention Shabbat or kashrut at all, and observant readers are usually left with an open question: is this dream for me too? This guide answers that question in detail. It explains how such a journey is scheduled, what you eat and where, how to pray at altitude, and what to ask a rabbi before you leave. If you are considering the highest mountain in Africa and Shabbat is part of your life, this is the place to start.

content.value: The problem: a mountain that does not stop for Shabbat

Climbing Kilimanjaro means continuous movement. Every day you move from camp to camp, the tents come down in the morning and go up again in the evening, and a crew of guides, cooks and porters moves with the group. The standard routes have no rest day in one place, and even if they did, Shabbat in a tent at 4,000 m, with no eruv, no synagogue and no way to warm food, would be a very hard Shabbat.

So the solution is not to try to stop the mountain for Shabbat, but to build the journey so that Shabbat falls outside the park. That requires a route of precise length, one that starts on Sunday and finishes on Friday before midday, while still giving the body enough days to acclimatize. A route that is too short hurts the chances of reaching the summit. A route that is too long runs into Shabbat.
How to fit a climb between two Shabbatot
HighAir's Shabbat-observant expedition lasts 10 days and is built around two full Shabbatot in Arusha, the large town at the foot of the mountain. This is how it looks, day by day:

items: Friday: landing at Kilimanjaro International Airport, a drive of about two hours to Arusha, and Friday night dinner at Chabad House Arusha.
Shabbat: rest at the hotel. A quiet day before setting out, which also helps the body recover from the flight.
Sunday: Machame Gate (1,800 m) to Machame Camp (2,835 m), through the rainforest.
Monday: up to Shira Camp (3,750 m).
Tuesday: up to Lava Tower (4,600 m) and down to sleep at Barranco Camp (3,900 m).
Wednesday: the Barranco Wall and the climb to Barafu Camp (4,673 m), the last camp before the summit.
Wednesday night and Thursday: departure at midnight for Uhuru Peak (5,895 m) and descent to Mweka Camp (3,100 m).
Friday: descent to Mweka Gate (1,640 m) and back to the hotel in Arusha before Shabbat begins.
Shabbat: rest and an end-of-climb celebration in Arusha.
Sunday: flight home, or departure for a safari.

content.value: Six days on the mountain, five nights in tents, and not one step on Shabbat. The route is Machame, the same route our standard groups climb, with the classic acclimatization principle of climbing high and sleeping low: on the third day you climb to 4,600 m and descend to sleep at 3,900 m, so the body learns the altitude before summit night.

content.title: ✦ Why it works
content.value: Sunday to Friday midday is exactly six trekking days. That is enough for reasonable acclimatization on Machame, and it leaves a margin of several hours before Shabbat even if the final descent takes longer.

An important point: in the mountains there is no promise of a summit, only a commitment to safety. If a participant needs to descend early because of altitude sickness or any other reason, they come down the mountain accompanied by the crew, and their Shabbat is spent at the hotel, exactly like the rest of the group, only a few days earlier.
Shabbat in Arusha

Arusha is the town from which most Kilimanjaro expeditions set out, and it is also one of the few places in northern Tanzania with organized Jewish life. Chabad of Arusha has operated in the town since 2021 and offers Shabbat meals, weekday kosher food and a kosher restaurant. In Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's largest city, a second Chabad center has operated since 2024.

On our expedition, the first Friday night dinner takes place at Chabad House, and the rest of Shabbat is spent at the hotel in Arusha. The second Shabbat, after coming down from the mountain, is a different Shabbat altogether: a good tiredness in the body, summit photos on the phone, and many stories around the table.
Shabbat times near the equator

Arusha lies about three degrees south of the equator, so the length of the day hardly changes through the year. Sunset in Arusha ranges from 18:24 in October to 18:53 in February. In practice this means Shabbat begins and ends at almost the same time in every season, which makes planning very easy. Check the exact candle lighting time for each Shabbat in advance with a location-based calendar or with the local Chabad House.

content.value: Kashrut on the mountain: what you eat at 4,000 m

There are no restaurants and no shops on Kilimanjaro. Everything eaten on the mountain goes up with you, on the porters' backs, and is cooked at camp by the kitchen crew. That is exactly what makes full kashrut possible: when the entire kitchen is set up for the group, you decide in advance what goes into it.

On the Shabbat-observant expedition, the three daily meals on the mountain are coordinated with Chabad of Arusha. The kitchen is separate, the utensils are separate, and the meat is slaughtered according to halacha. The food is cooked fresh at every camp, so even at four thousand meters there is a hot meal at the end of a day of walking.

Why does this matter more than it seems? Because appetite drops at altitude. Many climbers find it hard to eat exactly when the body needs the most energy. A hot, familiar, tasty meal is not a luxury, it is part of the chance of reaching the summit. Someone forced to live on packaged snacks brought from home arrives at summit night weaker.
What is still worth bringing from home

items: Energy bars and dried fruit with a hechsher you trust, to eat while walking.
Familiar drink powders or sweeteners, because water tastes different at altitude and drinking a lot is essential.
Wine or grape juice for kiddush, if you have a particular preference. Coordinate in advance what will be available in Arusha.
Any product you are personally strict about, such as chalav Yisrael or pat Yisrael, after coordinating with us in advance.

content.value: Prayer at altitude

The day on the mountain starts early. Wake up at first light, breakfast, a short medical check by the guides, and off you go. There is time for Shacharit before setting out, and in the afternoon, on arrival at camp, there is time for Mincha and Maariv before and after dinner. A Shabbat-observant group can pray together, and if there is a minyan, prayer at camp between the tents, facing the mountain, is one of the moments participants remember most.

A few practical points: tallit and tefillin need room in the large bag the porters carry, up to 15 kg per person, so pack them in a waterproof bag. At altitude it is warm by day and very cold at night, and the winter clothing you wear in the morning will be layer upon layer. A small, light prayer book is better than a heavy siddur.
Summit day: a question for your rabbi

Summit night is the most complex day in halachic terms. You leave Barafu Camp at midnight, walk for about eight hours in the dark and cold, and reach the summit around sunrise. When to pray Shacharit, how to manage tefillin in that cold and effort, and what to do if you arrive early or late: these are questions to ask a rabbi before you leave, not to solve at two in the morning at 5,000 m. We recommend every participant arrive with a clear answer from their own rabbi.

Many also ask about the blessing on seeing high mountains. That too is a good question for your rabbi before the trip. What is certain: anyone who stands on the roof of Africa at sunrise, with glaciers all around and clouds beneath their feet, understands why the words "how manifold are Your works" were written.

content.value: What it costs and what is included

The Shabbat-observant expedition costs 3,100 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Arusha and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 4 nights in a 4-star hotel in Arusha with breakfast, double tents with mattresses during the climb, three full meals a day throughout the climb in coordination with Chabad Arusha, professional local English-speaking guides, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, porters for the logistical equipment with a kitchen crew and waiters, private portable toilets for the group only, entry and climbing permits for Kilimanjaro National Park, a first aid kit with emergency oxygen cylinders, live WhatsApp updates for families during the climb, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the climb, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap and a dry-fit shirt, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with high-altitude evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Arusha, personal gear (clothing and footwear), tips for the climbing crew (300 dollars per person), the Tanzania visa (50 dollars), the local government insurance (44 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. The full breakdown, including extras such as a single room or a solo tent, is on the expedition page. We have written separate guides on the visa and on money in Tanzania.
Who it suits

Kilimanjaro requires no technical climbing experience. There are no ropes, no crampons and no ice walls. What it requires is good aerobic fitness, the ability to walk for many hours a day, several days in a row, and above all the patience to climb slowly. The minimum age in the park is 10, accompanied by a parent or an adult. A medical certificate and health declaration are required from every participant before departure.

The Shabbat-observant expedition suits observant travelers of every background, couples, parents with adult children, and anyone who simply wants to climb with a group that shares their values. The group is limited to 15 participants. The preferred seasons are January to February and June to October, the drier months on the mountain. It is also worth checking with a travel clinic which vaccinations you need, and we have written a separate guide on that.

Good to know: the climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups on the mountain. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having.
Kosher Kilimanjaro with HighAir

At HighAir we take groups to Kilimanjaro every year, and the Shabbat-observant expedition answers one question: "Is this possible for me too?" The answer is yes. The route, the guides and the pace are the same as our standard groups, and the success rate we publish for this route is 94 percent. The difference is a schedule built around Shabbat, a kosher kitchen and the atmosphere of a group that prays together.

After the second Shabbat you can fly home, or add three safari days in Tarangire and the Ngorongoro Crater. Anyone who prefers a different date or more flexibility can also look at our standard Kilimanjaro expeditions.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see today on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain. If this is your mountain, and Shabbat matters to you, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
Can you climb Kilimanjaro without breaking Shabbat?

Yes. HighAir's Shabbat-observant expedition is built so that all climbing days fall between Sunday and Friday midday. Both Shabbatot of the trip are spent at the hotel in Arusha, and the first includes Friday night dinner at Chabad House. There is no walking, driving or climbing on Shabbat.
Is the food on the mountain kosher?

Yes. The three daily meals on the mountain are coordinated with Chabad of Arusha, with a separate kitchen, separate utensils and meat slaughtered according to halacha. The food is cooked fresh at every camp. Anyone with additional personal stringencies is welcome to coordinate with us in advance.
How many days does the kosher Kilimanjaro climb take?
The whole journey lasts 10 days: Shabbat in Arusha, six climbing days on the Machame route, a second Shabbat in Arusha and a travel day. Three safari days can be added after the second Shabbat.
Is there a Chabad House in Arusha?

Yes. Chabad of Arusha has operated in the town since 2021 and offers Shabbat meals and kosher food. A second Chabad center has operated in Dar es Salaam since 2024. Check current opening hours with them before you travel.
When does Shabbat start in Tanzania?

Arusha is close to the equator, so sunset is almost constant through the year, roughly between 18:20 and 18:55 depending on the season. Check the exact candle lighting time for each Shabbat with a location-based calendar or with the local Chabad House.
How do you pray on summit day?

On summit day you leave at midnight and reach the summit around sunrise, so prayer times and tefillin need planning in advance. We recommend every participant ask their own rabbi before the trip and arrive with clear guidance. On the other days there is time for Shacharit before setting out and for Mincha and Maariv at camp.
What language do the guides speak?
The climb is led by professional local guides who speak English and have long experience leading groups on Kilimanjaro. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having.
